Rm(T)=0.30(T3​keV)1/2gcm−2,R_{m}(T)=0.30\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{T}{3~\mathrm{keV}}}}\right)^{1/2}~\mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}}, (III.9)

consistent with 3.5 MeV alpha stopping data. Deposition was limited to 90%90\% of total energy (fdep≤0.9f_{\text{dep}}\leq 0.9) to mimic escape.

Finally, for radiation losses, we use an approximate gray diffusion with an escape probability [50, 16]:

Qrad=Crad​ρ2​T​11+κ0​ρ​Rout,Q_{\text{rad}}=C_{\text{rad}}\,\rho^{2}\sqrt{T}\,\frac{1}{1+\kappa_{0}\rho R_{\text{out}}}, (III.10)

where Crad=3×10−36​W​m3​kg−2​keV−1/2C_{\text{rad}}=3\times 10^{-36}~\mathrm{W\,m^{3}\,kg^{-2}\,keV^{-1/2}} and κ0=5×10−3\kappa_{0}=5\times 10^{-3} approximate Rosseland mean opacities for DT.

GPT-5 is quite good at this kind of model development and setup. It required little intervention on my part to make this plausible and complete. That would change in the numerics.

III.3.3 Numerical Implementation

GPT-5, without explicit prompting, selected for a partial differential equation (PDE) solving a second-order Crank–Nicolson implicit scheme on a uniform radial grid (N≈150N\approx 150 points). Time integration proceeded with adaptive substeps up to 10 ns. Boundary conditions:

∂T∂r=0at ​r=0,∂T∂r=0at ​r=Router.\frac{\partial T}{\partial r}=0\quad\text{at }r=0,\qquad\frac{\partial T}{\partial r}=0\quad\text{at }r=R_{\text{outer}}. (III.11)

Reaction, diffusion, and radiative source terms were split via operator splitting. Alpha deposition was solved by a tridiagonal Helmholtz inversion at each step.

These are reasonable choices for the kind of testbed we seek to develop. It should be noted that this took a few minutes to code up. While I could have done this, I do not do it every day, and I suspect it would have taken me a few work days to really get solid code working. The point is that I can now deliver in minutes as if I were at the highest level I have ever been at for this kind of work. There are those who will say this implementation is not remarkable, and it is not. But, to have it in minutes is remarkable.

It was at this point that my human labor and intelligence were required. I needed to suggest some parameterization for the density and temperature profiles at the fusion boundary. GPT-5 also needed me to help it find the region of parameter space that exhibited the kinds of threshold behaviors we were looking for. Make the hot spot too strong, and the whole thing singularly explodes. Make it too weak, and no burn wave will initiate and propagate. To understand the effect of the profile we are imagining, we need a delicately balanced marginal system. Given the nonlinearities in ICF, this takes not only intuition, but some numerical empiricism. GPT-5 made me work here.

For the density profile, three regions were specified:

  • •

    Region 1 (hot spot): r≤Rh​sr\leq R_{hs}, ρ=ρh​s≈1.2​g​cm−3\rho=\rho_{hs}\approx 1.2~\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

  • •

    Region 2 (ramp): Rh​s<r≤Rh​s+LrampR_{hs}<r\leq R_{hs}+L_{\text{ramp}},

    ρ​(r)=ρh​s+s​(r−Rh​s)+c​(r−Rh​s)2,\rho(r)=\rho_{hs}+s(r-R_{hs})+c(r-R_{hs})^{2}, (III.12)

    scaled to ensure ρ​(Rh​s+Lramp)=ρcold\rho(R_{hs}+L_{\text{ramp}})=\rho_{\text{cold}}.

  • •

    Region 3 (cold fuel): ρ=ρcold≈150​g​cm−3\rho=\rho_{\text{cold}}\approx 150~\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

The ramp is controlled by the slope ss and curvature cc, spanning

s∈[1.5,6.5]×109​kg​m−4andc∈[−6.5,0]×1013​kg​m−5.s\in[1.5,6.5]\times 10^{9}~\mathrm{kg\,m^{-4}}\quad\text{and}\quad c\in[-6.5,0]\times 10^{13}~\mathrm{kg\,m^{-5}}.

I spent a few hours of my time adjusting hot spot conditions, cold fuel conditions, conductivities, alpha particle stopping powers, and profile designs to get a physically reasonable result. This activity is what we in ICF might call “design work” – getting to the place where the physics are interesting and useful. GPT-5 was a bad designer, offering results that were null, noisy, or invalid (NaNs), while claiming that glory had been achieved. However, when re-prompted to examine a pathological result or null signal, GPT-5 offered quite sophisticated solutions, including different implementations of FFTs to prevent aliasing, improved resolutions to track burn fronts, altered performance metrics to amplify signals. If a user gave up at the first wacky response, they would miss out on some rather powerful capability of the model. It needs to be highlighted that this requires you to be a very confident physicist. You have to know that an assertion is wrong, you have to confidently push for a better solution, and you have to be good enough to know when a real solution has been reached. I often find that GPT-5 offers solutions that I have to think deeply about to determine if they are actually correct, or just convenient.

We settled on simulations that were performed at a fixed hot-spot temperature Th​s=1.5​keVT_{hs}=1.5~\mathrm{keV}. For each (slope, curvature) pair, the mean front speed of the 5 keV isotherm between 1–3 ns was measured by least-squares fitting:

vmean=∫t0t1d​rfd​t​𝑑tt1−t0.v_{\text{mean}}=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\frac{dr_{f}}{dt}\,dt}{t_{1}-t_{0}}. (III.13)

The resulting vmean​(s,c)v_{\text{mean}}(s,c) field was smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (10% bandwidth) to remove interpolation noise. Contours of 40–100 km s-1 clearly revealed a propagation ridge centered around

s≈3.0×109​kg​m−4,c≈−4.5×1013​kg​m−5,s^{\mathclose{}\,\mathopen{}}\approx 3.0\times 10^{9}~\mathrm{kg\,m^{-4}},\qquad c^{\mathclose{}\,\mathopen{}}\approx-4.5\times 10^{13}~\mathrm{kg\,m^{-5}}, (III.14)

with local maxima up to vmean≈100​km​s−1v_{\text{mean}}\approx 100~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}.

We spent some time examining the density profiles along the ridge. Five equally spaced points along this ridge were selected; their parameters are listed in Table III.1.

Figure III.1 illustrates that as curvature becomes less negative, the density near the hot-spot boundary rises faster – stiffening the thermal coupling and slightly reducing the front speed. Optimal profiles exhibit a gentle initial density rise, allowing alphas to preheat the ramp before losses dominate deeper in the cold fuel.

Within a few hours of noodling, we had a decent numerical picture of a relationship between the parameters chosen to describe the interface and their optimal values for propagating rapid burn fronts.

III.3.4 Theoretical Explanation

While the numerics show a trend, a good design physicist will aim to explain that trend using the theoretical tools at his disposal. I asked GPT-5 to help do this here for two reasons. First, it is useful to have this theoretical picture for forming the intuition we are looking for. Second, it provides an alternative check that GPT-5 has not hallucinated the physics and that I have not been fooled. This is a much-needed verification process.

GPT-5 quite quickly settled (following my nudging prompt) on a traveling-wave power balance to understand what sets the ridge.

We settled on a quasi–steady burn front, written in a co-moving coordinate ξ=r−v​t\xi=r-vt. Writing ρ=ρ​(ξ)\rho=\rho(\xi) from the imposed ramp, the energy equation reads

−vρCvd​Td​ξ=dd​ξ(ρχ(T,ρ)d​Td​ξ)+Qα[T,ρ;ρ(⋅)]−Qrad(T,ρ,ρRout).-v\,\rho C_{v}\,\frac{dT}{d\xi}=\frac{d}{d\xi}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\rho\,\chi(T,\rho)\,\frac{dT}{d\xi}}}\right)+Q_{\alpha}\bigl[T,\rho;\rho(\cdot)\bigr]-Q_{\mathrm{rad}}\bigl(T,\rho,\rho R_{\rm out}\bigr). (III.15)

It identified, I believe correctly, key scalings:

  • •

    Thermal transport: χ∼χ0​T5/2/ρ\chi\sim\chi_{0}T^{5/2}/\rho. Low ρ\rho implies strong preheat (large χ\chi), but also dilute heat capacity (smaller ρ​Cv\rho C_{v}).

  • •

    Fusion source: Qα∼fα​Efus​(nD​nT)​⟨σ​v⟩​(T)​𝒟​[ρ]Q_{\alpha}\sim f_{\alpha}E_{\rm fus}(n_{D}n_{T})\langle\sigma v\rangle(T)\,\mathcal{D}[\rho]. With n∝ρn\propto\rho, this gives Qα∝ρ2​⟨σ​v⟩​(T)Q_{\alpha}\propto\rho^{2}\langle\sigma v\rangle(T) times a nonlocal deposition factor 𝒟​[ρ]\mathcal{D}[\rho].

  • •

    Radiation losses: Qrad∼Crad​ρ2​T/(1+κ0​ρ​Rout)Q_{\rm rad}\sim C_{\rm rad}\rho^{2}\sqrt{T}/(1+\kappa_{0}\rho R_{\rm out}). Higher ρ\rho amplifies emissivity but also increases optical depth and reduces escape.

The ridge (maximal mean front speed) consists of (s,c)(s,c) pairs for which the net power into the preheat zone – from conduction plus alpha deposition – most efficiently overcomes radiative loss and the enthalpy needed to lift cold fuel to the 5 keV ignition threshold. In other words, where

(conduction from hot side)+(nonlocal alpha deposition)⏟effective drive​is maximized against​(radiative loss)+(downstream conduction)+ρ​Cv​v​Δ​T⏟sinks + enthalpy\underbrace{\begin{array}[]{l}\text{(conduction from hot side)}\,+\\ \text{(nonlocal alpha deposition)}\end{array}}_{\text{effective drive}}\;\;\;\text{is maximized against}\;\;\;\underbrace{\begin{array}[]{l}\text{(radiative loss)}\,+\\ \text{(downstream conduction)}\,+\\ \rho C_{v}v\Delta T\end{array}}_{\text{sinks + enthalpy}} (III.16)

It argued for an optimal slope ss. Write the ramp (endpoint-normalized) as

ρ​(ξ)≈ρhs+s​Δ+c​Δ2,Δ≡(ξ−ξhs)∈[0,Lramp].\rho(\xi)\approx\rho_{\rm hs}+s\,\Delta+c\,\Delta^{2},\quad\Delta\equiv(\xi-\xi_{\rm hs})\in[0,L_{\rm ramp}]. (III.17)

Make ss smaller (shallower): the near-front ρ\rho stays lower for longer distances.

  • •

    Pros: larger χ∝1/ρ\chi\propto 1/\rho implies better conductive reach; longer alpha stopping length λα∼Rm/ρ\lambda_{\alpha}\sim R_{m}/\rho implies alphas preheat ahead of the front.

  • •

    Cons: Qα∝ρ2Q_{\alpha}\propto\rho^{2} is weaker at the front; also the hot preheat layer is optically thinner, so radiative escape improves.

Make ss larger (steeper): the front sees higher ρ\rho sooner.

  • •

    Pros: stronger Qα∝ρ2Q_{\alpha}\propto\rho^{2}, larger heat capacity ρ​Cv\rho C_{v} to “catch and hold” heat, greater ρ​R\rho R so alpha energy deposits more locally (bigger fdepf_{\rm dep}).

  • •

    Cons: χ\chi falls as 1/ρ1/\rho, so preheat is poorer; emissivity (∝ρ2\propto\rho^{2}) rises, giving a larger radiative sink (even if escape probability shrinks).

Net: there is a sweet spot in ss where conductive/alpha reach is still good, but ρ\rho at the front is just high enough to bootstrap self-heating without being overly lossy.

It then moved on to optimal curvature cc and why “moderately negative” values win.

Curvature redistributes where along the ramp the density rises:

  • •

    Negative curvature (c<0c<0) produces a gentle initial rise near the hot-spot edge and a steeper rise later. This creates a “preheat shelf”: a low-ρ\rho, optically thinner, high-χ\chi region right where alpha deposition from the hot spot wants to land (a few λα\lambda_{\alpha} out). It boosts nonlocal alpha coupling and conductive lift to 5 keV in the ramp before losses take over.

  • •

    Positive curvature (c>0c>0) produces a steep early rise that quickly increases ρ\rho just outside the hot spot. That chokes preheat (low χ\chi), increases emissivity, and shortens λα\lambda_{\alpha} so more alpha energy deposits behind the front rather than ahead of it – good for peak TT behind, bad for front advance.

This is why the data favor moderately negative curvature at nearly any slope that lies on the ridge: it positions the right ρ\rho at the right distance so the alpha–conduction synergy is maximized where the front needs it.

Ultimately, a simple power-balance criterion predicts an “ideal” cc for each ss. A helpful mental model is to focus on a control volume of thickness δ\delta centered a distance Δ⋆\Delta^{\star} ahead of the hot-spot edge, where the front is forming. Choose Δ⋆∼\Delta^{\star}\sim a few local alpha ranges and conductive penetration depths during 1–3 ns. Then require net positive power there to reach and hold Tig≈5​keVT_{\rm ig}\approx 5~\mathrm{keV}:

Qαin​(Δ⋆)⏟nonlocal from hot side+Qcondin​(Δ⋆)⏟∝χ​Δ​T/ℓ≳Qrad​(ρ​(Δ⋆),T)⏟∝ρ​(Δ⋆)2​T/(1+κ0​ρ​Rout)+ρ​(Δ⋆)​Cv​Tig−T0τ⏟enthalpy over timescale ​τ.\underbrace{Q_{\alpha}^{\rm in}(\Delta^{\star})}_{\text{nonlocal from hot side}}+\underbrace{Q_{\rm cond}^{\rm in}(\Delta^{\star})}_{\propto\chi\,\Delta T/\ell}\gtrsim\underbrace{Q_{\rm rad}(\rho(\Delta^{\star}),T)}_{\propto\rho(\Delta^{\star})^{2}\sqrt{T}/(1+\kappa_{0}\rho R_{\rm out})}+\underbrace{\rho(\Delta^{\star})C_{v}\frac{T_{\rm ig}-T_{0}}{\tau}}_{\text{enthalpy over timescale }\tau}. (III.18)

Two closure relations connect ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}) to (s,c)(s,c):

  • •

    Alpha reach: λα​(Δ⋆)∼Rm/ρ​(Δ⋆)\lambda_{\alpha}(\Delta^{\star})\sim R_{m}/\rho(\Delta^{\star}) should be commensurate with Δ⋆\Delta^{\star}, otherwise alphas either overshoot (too low ρ\rho) or deposit behind (too high ρ\rho):

    ρ​(Δ⋆)​Δ⋆∼Rm(order unity in areal density).\rho(\Delta^{\star})\,\Delta^{\star}\sim R_{m}\quad\text{(order unity in areal density)}. (III.19)

    For a fixed ss, this picks out a ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}) and thus fixes the needed curvature cc via ρ​(Δ⋆)=ρhs+s​Δ⋆+c​Δ⋆2\rho(\Delta^{\star})=\rho_{\rm hs}+s\,\Delta^{\star}+c\,{\Delta^{\star}}^{2}.

  • •

    Conduction match: the conductive preheat length in time τ\tau is ℓc∼χ​τ∼(χ0​T5/2/ρ)​τ\ell_{c}\sim\sqrt{\chi\,\tau}\sim\sqrt{(\chi_{0}T^{5/2}/\rho)\tau}. Efficient preheat wants ℓc∼Δ⋆\ell_{c}\sim\Delta^{\star}, i.e.

    χ0​T5/2ρ​(Δ⋆)∼Δ⋆2τ.\frac{\chi_{0}T^{5/2}}{\rho(\Delta^{\star})}\sim\frac{{\Delta^{\star}}^{2}}{\tau}. (III.20)

    This again fixes ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}) (hence cc) at a given ss and τ\tau (1–3 ns in our metric).

Put together, for each slope ss there is a best ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}) that simultaneously (i) matches alpha areal-range (ρ​Δ⋆∼Rm\rho\Delta^{\star}\sim R_{m}) and (ii) conductive reach (ℓc∼Δ⋆\ell_{c}\sim\Delta^{\star}). Because cc is the degree of freedom that reshapes ρ​(Δ)\rho(\Delta) locally at Δ⋆\Delta^{\star} while keeping the ramp endpoint fixed, you get an ideal curvature c⋆​(s)c^{\star}(s). This c⋆​(s)c^{\star}(s) traces the observed ridge.

Intuition from that criterion:

  • •

    If ss is too shallow, ρ​(Δ)\rho(\Delta) stays small; you need a less negative cc (or even positive) to raise ρ\rho at Δ⋆\Delta^{\star} enough to meet ρ​Δ⋆∼Rm\rho\Delta^{\star}\sim R_{m}.

  • •

    If ss is too steep, ρ​(Δ)\rho(\Delta) climbs quickly; you need more negative cc to delay the rise so alphas/conduction can reach and heat ahead of the front before losses spike.

The ridge curvature is thus the locus where ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}) hits the Goldilocks window: big enough for QαQ_{\alpha} and confinement, small enough for reach and low radiative drain.

We also developed tests to be sure we were clear about how the ridge should shift with physics knobs.

This picture immediately predicts how the ridge moves if you change microphysics:

  • •

    Longer alpha range RmR_{m}: pushes the optimum toward shallower ss and more negative cc (to keep ρ​Δ⋆∼Rm\rho\Delta^{\star}\sim R_{m}).

  • •

    Stronger radiation (larger CradC_{\rm rad} or lower opacity): favors shallower densities near the front, so more negative cc at a given ss.

  • •

    Lower hot-spot temperature: reduces source, so the optimum shifts toward slightly larger ss (more ρ\rho where the front forms) but still prefers negative cc to preserve reach.

Finally, we ended with a compact “engineering rule.” Pick a target preheat distance Δ⋆\Delta^{\star} tied to your timing window (e.g., 1–3 ns) and desired 5 keV crossing. Then design (s,c)(s,c) so that

ρ​(Δ⋆)​Δ⋆≈Rmandχ0​Tig5/2ρ​(Δ⋆)≈Δ⋆2τ.\rho(\Delta^{\star})\,\Delta^{\star}\approx R_{m}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\chi_{0}T_{\rm ig}^{5/2}}{\rho(\Delta^{\star})}\approx\frac{{\Delta^{\star}}^{2}}{\tau}. (III.21)

This reduces to a single condition on ρ​(Δ⋆)\rho(\Delta^{\star}), hence a curvature c⋆c^{\star} at each slope ss. In practice you will land on shallow slopes with moderately negative curvature, exactly what the simulations highlighted.

This formula offers a check on our results, using microphysics and power balance to estimate the expected c⋆​(s)c^{\star}(s) relationship. As shown in Figure III.2, the red engineering rule and the numerically obtained ridge are pretty close. I invested about 6 hours in this project (it is quite interesting, but the exercise was to be quick), and I ended with both a numerical result and a theoretical explanation that give me confidence to proceed. As I mentioned earlier, this process itself is not novel. It is the workflow of a design physicist operating in the cutting-edge field of ICF. However, executing this workflow from concept, to numerical exploration, to theoretical supporting statement in hours is rather amazing.

III.3.5 Physics Conclusions and Study Outcomes

At the outset, I was looking for a set of physics goals, and we delivered:

  • •

    A static, 1-D spherical reaction–diffusion model captures the essential burn-wave physics of ICF hot-spot ignition and propagation.

  • •

    Including realistic alpha stopping and nonlocal deposition with gray radiative loss yields credible propagation thresholds (marginal ignition near 1 keV).

  • •

    The ridge analysis identifies a family of fuel ramps – shallow slope, moderately negative curvature – that maximize front speed at fixed Th​sT_{hs}.

  • •

    A theoretical analysis explains the ridge in density profile space from a fundamental power balance in a co-moving wave front.

  • •

    The resulting framework serves as a physics-informed testbed for developing theory, validating higher-fidelity hydrodynamic simulations, and designing future experiments.

This is a representative use of GPT-5 for my experience. The model took the seed of an idea that I had – a static model to get a feel for key physics at the initiation and propagation of a thermonuclear burn wave – and it helped me very quickly build a partial differential equation representation of the model. On command, it incorporated detailed stopping power and familiar (to the expert) physical data known to the ICF community. It discretized the problem, set up the optimization routine I imagined, and delivered the result I thought we would expect. This took me about 6 hours from start to finish – idea to writing. There is not too much expertise that I could not find by querying my colleagues at the national labs, doing internet search, deriving some things by hand, recalling some undergraduate and graduate numerical tricks, and writing a few hundred lines of code. And, that is amazing. It made me a one-person army of experts all rolled up, as if I were the best I had ever been at everything I have ever thought about ICF. I can name the world experts it felt like I was talking to or the ones I would have had to reach out to to help me with some small step. But, they were right there in my laptop (more or less).

The theoretical explanation that I worked up with it is probably the best part. This explanation directly ties known physics relations together to give a closed-form predictor of what we had already found. This is a good way of ensuring that the results built over hours of elicitation with the model are not wrong and that the model had not seduced me into buying its arguments.

The results, I must say, do not come without work. The model, in its eagerness to please, often introduces numerical duct tape to smooth over a thorny issue, silently swaps out detailed numerical solves for approximations with trends it knows I want, and confidently declares victory when numerical signals are still obviously noise. When pointed to these errors and unwanted outcomes, the model is very good at actually fixing the issue. But, users must be expert enough to catch the oversimplifications, must persist to get the model to reconsider, and must be vigilant to ensure that the refined results are driving in the right direction.

Overall, as I have noted many times, I feel like my 6 hours of work here yielded something I could have done over a month or two with a very good pair of postdocs – one for theory and one for numerics. So, say 6 person-months reduced to 6 person-hours. That is a compression of about a factor of 1000. I can only imagine what two postdocs and I could do if we collaborated with each of us working in this AI-accelerated mode.

Below is the complete Python code used to generate the Gaussian-smoothed ridge map and extract the five density profiles.

Chapter IV  New scientific results obtained with AI

IV.1 Erdős problems (part 2/2) – Mehtaab Sawhney and Mark Sellke

We continue from where we left off in Section LABEL:sec:09-05 and explain how GPT-5 Pro assisted us in solving Erdős Problem #848.

IV.1.1 AI–assisted solution to Problem #848

Erdős Problem #848 is in combinatorial number theory, and was posted as Problem 23 in [31]. This problem was genuinely open, and has now been solved by the first author and GPT-5, in combination with online comments of van Doorn, Weisenberg and Cambie. The statement is:

Problem #848: Let AA be a subset {1,2,…,N}\{1,2,\dots,N\} such that a​b+1ab+1 is not squarefree for all a,b∈Aa,b\in A (i.e. a​b+1ab+1 must be divisble by p2p^{2} for at least one prime pp). Then for all sufficiently large NN, no such set AA has more elements than A={1≤a≤N:a≡7(mod25)}A=\{1\leq a\leq N~:~a\equiv 7\pmod{25}\}.

Of course, the given set AA satisfies the desired property because 72+1≡0(mod25)7^{2}+1\equiv 0\pmod{25}. It further turns out that this maximal AA is unique except when {1≤a≤N:a≡18(mod25)}\{1\leq a\leq N~:~a\equiv 18\pmod{25}\} has the same size, and for some ε>0\varepsilon>0 any AA containing at least (1−ε)​N25\frac{(1-\varepsilon)N}{25} elements must be contained in one of these two. A full solution of this problem is included in the appendix.

This question is in a line of extremal questions raised by Erdős at the intersection of elementary number theory and combinatorics. For instance, Erdős and Silverman asked what is the densest subset of [N][N] such that A+AA+A avoids a perfect square; this was solved by [44] who showed that |A|≤(11/32+o​(1))​N|A|\leq(11/32+o(1))N. Erdős similarly asked (also within Problem 23 of [31]) about the largest collection A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N] such that a​bab is never square–free.

The starting point of the solution is to observe that the diagonal constraint that a2+1a^{2}+1 not be squarefree already places a substantial restriction on AA. Indeed, classical number theory implies that only primes p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4} can divide a2+1a^{2}+1 twice, and for each such prime only 2/p22/p^{2} fraction of integers aa have a2+1a^{2}+1 divisible by pp. Since divisibility by powers of different primes behaves approximately independently, this already implies the simple upper bound

1−∏p​ prime,p≡1​(mod 4)(1−2p2)≈0.1051-\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\text{ prime},\\ p\equiv 1\text{(mod 4)}\end{subarray}}\Big(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}}\Big)\approx 0.105

for the density of AA, which is within a factor of 33 of the truth.

What is more challenging is to use the off-diagonal constraints on a​b+1ab+1 to non-trivially improve this upper bound. For this the first author asked GPT-5 Pro for suggestions, via the prompt displayed in Figure IV.1 below (which itself built on online comments of van Doorn, Weisenberg and Cambie).

The idea suggested by GPT-5’s reply in Figure IV.1 gives a method to use any single number b∈Ab\in A to obtain similarly harsh constraints on all other a∈Aa\in A. For example, let A∗A^{\ast} be the subset of AA consisting of numbers congruent to neither 77 nor 1818 mod 2525. If A∗A^{\ast} is non-empty, then fixing any b∈A∗b\in A^{\ast}, we have for any a∈Aa\in A that both a2+1a^{2}+1 or a​b+1ab+1 must be divisible by p2p^{2} for some prime pp. But since b∈A∗b\in A^{\ast} it follows that only one of them can be divisible by 55 itself. This is a much stronger restriction on a∈Aa\in A and already yields the improved bound:

(2325)\displaystyle\Big(\frac{23}{25}\Big) (1−∏p≡1(mod4)p≥13(1−2p2))+225​(1−∏p≠5(1−1p2))\displaystyle\Big(1-\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\equiv 1\pmod{4}\\ p\geq 13\end{subarray}}\Big(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}}\Big)\Big)+\frac{2}{25}\Big(1-\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq 5\end{subarray}}\Big(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}}\Big)\Big)
≤.02517+.0294≈.05457.\displaystyle\leq.02517+.0294\approx.05457.

Indeed for the (23/25)(23/25)-fraction of integers not congruent to 77 or 1818 mod 2525 we apply the diagonal argument above, and if a≡7,18(mod25)a\equiv 7,18\pmod{25} then a​b+1ab+1 must be divisible by p2p^{2} for p≠5p\neq 5. This bound is already not far from the truth, which suggests that pushing it further ought to solve the entire problem. GPT-5 made attempts in this direction but had numerous errors in its implementation (as can be seen in the transcript). Still, the high-level idea was sound and was quickly turned into a complete proof.

A first step of the eventual solution was to note that if b∈A∗b\in A^{\ast} is moreover even, then a​b+1ab+1 cannot be divisible by 44 and so the bound above improves to

(2325)\displaystyle\Big(\frac{23}{25}\Big) (1−∏p≡1(mod4)p≥13(1−2p2))+225​(1−∏p∉{2,5}(1−1p2))\displaystyle\Big(1-\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\equiv 1\pmod{4}\\ p\geq 13\end{subarray}}(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}})\Big)+\frac{2}{25}\Big(1-\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\notin\{2,5\}\end{subarray}}(1-\frac{1}{p^{2}})\Big)
≤.02517+.0125≈.03767.\displaystyle\leq.02517+.0125\approx.03767.

Since .03767<1/25.03767<1/25 is strictly smaller than the density of numbers 77 mod 2525, this already implies that a near-maximal set AA cannot contain any even numbers in A∗A^{\ast} at all. Further casework in this vein allows one to rule out the existence of any b∈A∗b\in A^{\ast} whatsoever, and finally to show that mixing between 77 and 1818 mod 2525 is inefficient as well. The main discussion with GPT-5 can be found here: [60].

We emphasize that the first observation mentioned is due to Wouter van Doorn and the particular prompt given to GPT-5 was based on a comment of Stijn Cambie; these were already present in the comments of the official website https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/848. Thus, the final proof consists of a key solution step due to GPT-5 sandwiched between two layers of human mathematics!

IV.1.2 Looking Forward

Our investigation of Erdős problem #848 highlights that GPT-5 has the ability to serve as an effective mathematical assistant, capable of recalling relevant lemmas, identifying analogies and locating relevant results from vague, ill-specified prompts. However, current models remain limited in perceiving the “negative space” of mathematics. While models are able to suggest plausible proof strategies, they often do not realize certain “obvious” examples which block progress, and are overly confident in the power of existing methods. This is unsurprising as such discussion is largely absent in mathematical literature itself; mathematicians don’t systematically record why problems are out reach, or why a more obvious strategy doesn’t work, or why certain techniques are inherently unable to solve certain classes of problems.

IV.1.3 Formal solution of Problem #848

Proposition IV.1.1.

There exists an integer N0N_{0} such that if N≥N0N\geq N_{0} then the following holds. Let A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N] with the property that if a,b∈Aa,b\in A then a​b+1ab+1 is not squarefree. Then

|A|≤|{n∈[N]:n≡7(mod25)}|,|A|\leq|\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\}|,

i.e. {n∈[N]:n≡7(mod25)}\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\} achieves the maximum possible value of |A||A|.

Remark IV.1.1.

Our proof actually allows one to go further and characterize all approximately maximal sets AA. Namely equality is achieved precisely when A={n∈[N]:n≡7(mod25)}A=\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\} or A={n∈[N]:n≡18(mod25)}A=\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 18\pmod{25}\} (the latter may be optimal or suboptimal by 11 depending on the value of nn modulo 2525). Further it turns out that for all |A|≥0.038⋅N|A|\geq 0.038\cdot N within 5%5\% of optimality, when NN is sufficiently large, AA must be contained in either {n∈[N]:n≡7(mod25)}\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\} or {n∈[N]:n≡18(mod25)}\{n\in[N]:n\equiv 18\pmod{25}\} (and of course all such AA satisfy the squarefree condition).

We first require the following pair of preliminary lemmas; the first was already used by van Doorn (see [14]). In order to be self-contained, we provide proofs with suboptimal error terms.

Lemma IV.1.1.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a subset of primes with max⁡𝒫≤N1/2\max\mathcal{P}\leq N^{1/2} and let qq be a positive integer. For each p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P}, define ℛp\mathcal{R}_{p} to denote a set of residue classes modulo p2p^{2} with |ℛp|≤2|\mathcal{R}_{p}|\leq 2 and ℛp=∅\mathcal{R}_{p}=\emptyset if (p,q)≠1(p,q)\neq 1. Then

||({n∈[N]:n≡tmodq}​⋂⋃p∈𝒫{n(modp2)∈ℛp})|−Nq​(1−∏p∈𝒫(1−|ℛp|p2))|\displaystyle\Bigg|\Big|\Big(\big\{n\in[N]:n\equiv t\mod q\big\}\bigcap\bigcup_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\{n\pmod{p^{2}}\in\mathcal{R}_{p}\}\Big)\Big|-\frac{N}{q}\Big(1-\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\Big(1-\frac{|\mathcal{R}_{p}|}{p^{2}}\Big)\Big)\Bigg|
≤O​(N​(log⁡N)−1/2).\displaystyle\leq O(N(\log N)^{-1/2}).
Proof.

Let T=⌊log⁡N⌋T=\lfloor\sqrt{\log N}\rfloor. Note that

|[N]​⋂⋃p∈𝒫T≤p≤N1/2{n(modp2)∈ℛp}|≤O​(∑T≤p≤N1/2Np2)≤O​(NT).\Big|[N]\bigcap\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in\mathcal{P}\\ T\leq p\leq N^{1/2}\end{subarray}}\{n\pmod{p^{2}}\in\mathcal{R}_{p}\}\Big|\leq O\Big(\sum_{T\leq p\leq N^{1/2}}\frac{N}{p^{2}}\Big)\leq O\Big(\frac{N}{T}\Big).

Note that as T≤log⁡NT\leq\sqrt{\log N}, we have that ∏p≤Tp2≤No​(1)\prod_{p\leq T}p^{2}\leq N^{o(1)}. Via inclusion exclusion, we have

|({n∈[N]:n≡tmodq}​⋂⋃p∈𝒫p≤T{n(modp2)∈ℛp})|\displaystyle\Big|\Big(\big\{n\in[N]:n\equiv t\mod q\big\}\bigcap\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in\mathcal{P}\\ p\leq T\end{subarray}}\{n\pmod{p^{2}}\in\mathcal{R}_{p}\}\Big)\Big|

We now give the remainder of the analysis to conclude the proof. The proof consists of breaking the set into the parts which are 7(mod25)7\pmod{25}, those that are 18(mod25)18\pmod{25}, and all the rest. We note that there exist other similar solutions within this framework; indeed our initial version of the solution required more extensive casework modulo numbers including 169169 and 289289. The conversation with GPT-5 [60] in particular uses the auxiliary prime 33 and therefore the precise computation differs from the draft here.

IV.2 New online algorithms lower bounds – Christian Coester

This section describes how GPT-5 assisted in proving new bounds on the performance of algorithms for a fundamental problem in online optimization called convex body chasing. The problem was introduced by [33] and captures how to make sequential decisions under uncertainty when each step restricts feasible options in a geometric way. Formally, one is given a sequence of convex sets K1,K2,…,KT⊂ℝdK_{1},K_{2},\ldots,K_{T}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, revealed one by one. Upon seeing KtK_{t}, an algorithm must choose a point pt∈Ktp_{t}\in K_{t} before learning the next set. The goal is to minimize the total movement ∑t=1T‖pt−pt−1‖\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|p_{t}-p_{t-1}\|. The algorithm is called online as it has to make decisions on the fly, without knowledge of the future. In contrast, an offline algorithm is one that knows the entire input upfront, allowing it to move optimally. The standard measure of performance of an online algorithm is its competitive ratio, defined as the worst-case (i.e., maximum) ratio between the online algorithm’s cost and the optimum (offline) cost on any instance.

Intuitively, convex body chasing formalizes the tension between adaptivity and stability: each new convex body represents a changing feasible region (e.g., updated constraints, new data, or evolving system state), and the online algorithm must adjust with minimal movement. It arises naturally in contexts like control theory (tracking feasible states), machine learning (online convex optimization with movement costs), and operations research (dynamic resource allocation). In theoretical computer science, it serves as a clean abstraction for understanding how well an online decision process can perform relative to an omniscient optimum, with close connections to other central problems in online optimization [8].

When introducing the problem, [33] showed that the competitive ratio of any online algorithm is at least d\sqrt{d} in dd-dimensional Euclidean space. Following a sequence of breakthroughs in recent years ([19, 5, 62]), it is now established that the optimal competitive ratio lies in the interval [d,d][\sqrt{d},d]. An important special case that received significant attention is chasing nested convex bodies, where K1⊃K2⊃⋯⊃KTK_{1}\supset K_{2}\supset\dots\supset K_{T} ([7, 4, 18]).

The following sections show how GPT-5 refuted competitiveness of a natural algorithm in response to a single prompt, and how it assisted in raising the lower bound on the competitive ratio of arbitrary online algorithms from d\sqrt{d} to π2​⌊d2⌋≈1.11​d\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor}\approx 1.11\sqrt{d}.

IV.2.1 Lower bound for Follow-the-Leader

When the initial location is p0=0p_{0}=0, observe that for nested convex body chasing, the optimal offline algorithm will move to arg⁡minp∈KT⁡‖p‖\arg\min_{p\in K_{T}}\|p\|, which is feasible for all time steps and minimizes cost. So a natural online algorithm is to move to pt=arg⁡minp∈Kt⁡‖p‖p_{t}=\arg\min_{p\in K_{t}}\|p\| at each time tt, i.e., tracking the currently optimal offline location. I did not necessarily expect this algorithm to perform well as this type of follow-the-leader algorithm is known to have poor competitive ratio for related problems, and the reason is typically trivial. However, I could not see any such easy argument to refute the algorithm, and what made me curious is that it does achieve the optimal competitive ratio of π/2\pi/2 on the specific hard instance described in Section IV.2.2 that yields a π/2\pi/2 lower bound for arbitrary algorithms in the two-dimensional case. Given a single short prompt, GPT-5 produced a rather non-obvious counter-example against the algorithm. It shows that the cost of the algorithm can be made arbitrarily large even in the two-dimensional nested case when the initial body is the unit ball around the start location (and thus proves that the competitive ratio is infinite, since the optimal offline cost is at most 1 here):

Figure IV.3 contains an illustration of the construction. GPT goes on to justify the feasibility of the construction: “We must verify that (1) holds not only for the immediate predecessor but for all earlier indices.” The argument it gives for this is actually incorrect, but a correct argument is easy to see: For s≥t+1s\geq t+1, we obtain (1) from the following chain of inequalities:

cos(∠​(ut,us))≥cos(∠​(ut,ut+1))=rtrt+1≥rtrs.\cos(\angle(u_{t},u_{s}))\geq\cos(\angle(u_{t},u_{t+1}))=\frac{r_{t}}{r_{t+1}}\geq\frac{r_{t}}{r_{s}}.

GPT completes the proof (within the same response) as shown in the next chat box. The first line in it contains a slight inaccuracy, since we need the inequality not only for |x|≤π/8|x|\leq\pi/8 but for |x|≤π/4|x|\leq\pi/4. It holds even in that case though, so the overall proof is not affected.

Thus the “follow‑the‑leader” cost can be made arbitrarily large while all requests stay nested inside the unit disk. The original interaction is available at [21].

IV.2.2 Improved lower bounds for general algorithms

We now discuss how GPT-5’s assistance helped in proving a better lower bound on the competitive ratio of arbitrary online algorithms. The idea for this lower bound is based on a previous 1.5358 lower bound due to [13] for chasing lines (i.e., where each KtK_{t} is a line), which was the only previous known improvement over the aforementioned d\sqrt{d} (when d=2d=2). The proof in [13] is rather ad-hoc, giving a small number of request lines issued in three steps, using six rational constants to specify those lines. It was acknowledged by [13] that 1.5358 does not seem to be tight, since a generalization of their idea, using more steps and request lines, should achieve a better bound. However, this would make their analysis even more involved.

My goal was to derive a better and cleaner lower bound using a generalization of their approach where the request line moves continuously. My initial attempts to prompt GPT-5 to help with this construction were unsuccessful: It only reproved the known 1.5358 lower bound, failing to understand why my suggested continuous generalization would be helpful. Curiously though, the reasoning trace preview mentioned at one point that it was aiming for a lower bound of π/2≈1.5708\pi/2\approx 1.5708, a quantity I had not thought of before (the prompt of Section IV.2.1 took place at a later time). Although the reasoning trace preview did not substantiate why it would aim for this number specifically, and the responses did not mention it any more, it may have contributed to inspiring me towards the following, more concrete plan for a lower bound:

Lower bound idea (see Figure IV.4).

Consider an instance with initial location (0,0)(0,0), each request set is a line, initially the line y=0y=0. Start rotating the line clockwise around B=(1,0)B=(1,0). Observe that the projection ptp_{t} of the origin onto the current line KtK_{t} is the north-western intersection of KtK_{t} with the circle of radius 1/21/2 around (1/2,0)(1/2,0). This is essentially due to Thales’ theorem. If the online algorithm follows this curve until the request line is vertical, then it moves along the semicircle and its cost is exactly π/2\pi/2 whereas the optimal cost is 11. So an algorithm has to deviate from this curve in order to achieve a smaller competitive ratio. In fact, since we can force the algorithm to end at BB, it has to go “below” the semicircle curve at some point, otherwise its path is even longer. Consider the first time tt when the online algorithm moves “below” the semicircle curve. Let B​’B’ be the intersection other than BB between KtK_{t} and the circle of radius 1 around the origin. Observe that ptp_{t} is the midpoint of the line segment B​B′¯\overline{BB^{\prime}}, and the minimal offline cost to reach any point x∈B​B′¯x\in\overline{BB^{\prime}} is the norm ‖x‖\|x\|, whose value is symmetric around ptp_{t} on B​B′¯\overline{BB^{\prime}}. So we can switch and pivot around B​’B’ instead of BB, counter-clockwise. The semicircle curve from before has a corresponding semicircle curve on the other side of ptp_{t}. The fact the online algorithm went “below” the previous semicircle curve means that it is now above/outside the new semicircle curve, and getting back onto the curve only makes it more expensive for the online algorithm. Repeating this argument, the algorithm should eventually reach a point ptp_{t} at distance 11 from the origin after having moved distance ≥π/2\geq\pi/2.

The task for GPT-5.

A subtle difficulty in the preceding argument lies in defining the precise moment of pivot switching. If the switch occurs exactly when the algorithm crosses below the semicircle, then at that moment the algorithm is still located on the semicircle, at the location where it intersects the new semicircle. But then it might also try to go below the new semicircle immediately, leading to a possibly infinite sequence of pivot switches at the same instant, effectively freezing the process.

My initial plan for resolving this was to argue that the algorithm must move at a temporarily faster speed in order to go below the semicircle, allowing the pivot switch to be delayed until its speed decreases again; but formalizing this approach seemed technically cumbersome. GPT-5 suggested a much simpler and cleaner solution: trigger the switch once the algorithm is below the semicircle at distance ≥ϵ\geq\epsilon from ptp_{t}. This avoids the freeze, and as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 we obtain the same lower bound of π/2\pi/2. This adjustment allows to make the argument rigorous and complete. The idea seems obvious in hindsight, yet far more elegant than the overcomplicated solution I was initially attempting. Since the interaction took place using Oxford’s ChatGPT Edu license, due to sharing restrictions of this license a link to the full interaction is unfortunately unavailable. An excerpt is shown in Figure IV.5.

Extension to higher dimension.

Finally, I was hoping to extend the lower bound to arbitrary dimension. My own approach (so far unsuccessful) was to first aim for an extension of the above idea to three dimensions, but it does not seem obvious how to do this. I posed the problem to GPT-5, with a prompt that included the lower bound idea above (without the ϵ\epsilon details) plus the following sentence:

Within its first response, GPT-5 proposed an approach yielding a lower bound of π2​⌊d2⌋≈1.11​d\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor}\approx 1.11\sqrt{d}. The idea is simple: Consider an orthogonal decomposition of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} into ⌊d/2⌋\lfloor d/2\rfloor two-dimensional components ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, and apply the π/2\pi/2 lower bound one by one in the components. Although there were errors in GPT-5’s proposed execution of this idea, it is not hard to make rigorous. The full chat is available at [22] (containing also subsequent unsuccessful attempts to push the ratio further). Notably, my initial focus on three dimensions might have caused me to miss this simple decomposition idea.

IV.2.3 Reflection

GPT-5 assisted the research process on this problem at several stages. Perhaps the most impressive part is its proof refuting the follow-the-leader algorithm, produced from a single prompt without any guidance on how to approach the task. This result saved significant time I might have otherwise spent unsuccessfully searching for an upper bound, and it is unclear if I would have been able to come up with the lower bound, which contained several non-trivial steps. The aid it provided for the lower bound on arbitrary algorithms was on the one hand the inspiring appearance of the number π/2\pi/2 in its reasoning trace, and on the other hand a technical idea to resolve the “freezing” issue in the proof. While I would have presumably found some solution to the freezing myself, it would have taken longer to formalize and likely been less elegant. GPT-5’s extension to arbitrary dimension was simple, but beyond the scope of my approach of focusing on three dimensions first.

Naturally, several limitations are also still apparent: it initially failed to understand how viewing the problem in continuous time could yield stronger bounds, and upon later attempts to push the lower bounds further, it presented arguments containing serious flaws. In the proofs presented in this section, GPT-5’s responses also contained some errors, but these were easy to fix for a human, overall accelerating the research process.

IV.3 Inequalities on subgraph counts in trees – Sébastien Bubeck, Mark Sellke, and Steven Yin

We conduct here another experiment, this time in graph theory, on a problem formulated and studied by the first author of this section, together with Nati Linial, in a 2013 preprint that was later published in 2016 in the Journal of Graph Theory ([20]). The paper lists 7 open problems, and the one we consider here is the first open problem, arguably the one we were most interested in solving back in 2013:

  • •

    The open problem is about a conjectured infinite set of inequalities for subgraph counts in trees, that if true would determine a certain convex set of interest.

  • •

    The follow-up paper [17] shows that, except possibly for the first two, none of these inequalities are actually true. Moreover the main result of [17] is a proof that the first inequality is indeed true. The second inequality is left as an open problem.

  • •

    Aided by somewhat sophisticated scaffolding (aimed at doing mathematics research), GPT-5 was able to reprove the first inequality, and then build on this to also prove the second (open) inequality. Both of GPT-5’s proofs are quite different from any of the arguments in [20, 17]. We present the re-proof of the first inequality in Section IV.3.2 and the new proof of the second in Section IV.3.3.

  • •

    Both proofs below are entirely AI-generated, aside from minor editing for clarity. No human input was needed beyond first asking to prove the first inequality, and then (with the solution to the first inequality in context) asking to prove the second inequality. (A few incorrect proofs were also generated and rejected by human checking.) See Figure IV.7 and Figure IV.8 for the precise prompts.

  • •

    We moreover note that GPT-5 did not have access to web search in this experiment, and did not seem to be aware of the existing proof in [17] (indeed the latter paper has remained quite niche, with only 3 citations in 10 years). The pre-existing (human-generated) proof rests on a somewhat cumbersome analysis, that analyzes several different cases across 4 pages of calculation. In contrast GPT-5’s proof is short and elegant, and based on a somewhat miraculous identity. The entire argument in Section IV.3.2 fits in a page and a half.

We note that we first attempted to use this research scaffolding on top of GPT-5 to solve a few Erdős problems, but with no success. The experiment described here was our first attempt at a problem outside of Erdős’ problems.

IV.3.1 Paths, stars and wyes in trees

Let GG be a finite tree. We consider the following subgraph counts (see also Figure IV.6):

  • •

    SS is the number of induced star subgraphs on 55 vertices within GG.

  • •

    PP is the number of induced path subgraphs on 55 vertices within GG.

  • •

    YY is the number of induced 55-vertex subtrees of the remaining isomorphism type within GG (i.e. 11 center vertex which is the endpoint of paths of lengths 1,1,21,1,2).

Theorem IV.3.1 ([17]).

For any finite tree GG, one has

Y−9​S−P≤6.Y-9S-P\leq 6. (IV.1)
Conjecture 1 ([20, 17]).

There exists some constant K>0K>0 such that for any finite tree GG, one has

29​Y−42​P−144​S≤K.29Y-42P-144S\leq K. (IV.2)

The motivation for the above problems is that the set of achievable asymptotic proportions (YY+S+P,SY+S+P,PY+S+P)\Big(\frac{Y}{Y+S+P},\frac{S}{Y+S+P},\frac{P}{Y+S+P}\Big) in trees as Y+S+P→∞Y+S+P\to\infty can be shown to be convex (in fact for general subtree counts); thus one would like to understand the linear constraints, and Theorem IV.3.1 appeared to be a tight example. By contrast in general (dense) graphs, it is known that the infinite-dimensional flag algebra semidefinite program of [55] generates all such inequalities, but that linear inequalities of the form above can still be computationally undecidable [38].

In some sense Theorem IV.3.1 gives the “first face" of this convex set, while Conjecture 1 gives the “second face". We note that Conjecture 1 was also made in [20], together with an infinite set of conjectured inequalities, one for each face, and those conjectured inequalities were all disproven in [17] except for Conjecture 1 which we will show here to be actually true.

Aside from being checked and rewritten for clarity, the new proofs below are entirely AI-generated.

IV.3.3 Proof of Conjecture 1

As mentioned above, the work [20] actually made an infinite sequence of conjectures parametrized by a positive integer C≥2C\geq 2 (each corresponding to a face of the convex set of achievable tree profiles), with the general statement that

C​(2​C2+7​C+7)​Y−C​(C+1)​(C2+3​C+4)​P−24​(C+1)​(C+2)​S≤O​(1)C(2C^{2}+7C+7)Y-C(C+1)(C^{2}+3C+4)P-24(C+1)(C+2)S\leq O(1)

for any fixed CC. In addition to confirming the case C=1C=1, [17] actually disproved this for C≥3C\geq 3. The same proof-oriented scaffolding on top of GPT-5 was able to confirm the remaining C=2C=2 case is true. The proof uses similar ideas but this time requires the non-positivity of a quite complicated non-polynomial function on the integers.

Theorem IV.3.2.

For any tree GG, one has

29​Y−42​P−144​S≤504.29Y-42P-144S\leq 504.

IV.4 COLT problem on dynamic networks – Sébastien Bubeck, Mark Sellke, and Steven Yin

We consider a random tree (Gt)t≥1(G_{t})_{t\geq 1} constructed iteratively as follows. At time t=1t=1 we begin with a single vertex. At each subsequent time t+1t+1, a new vertex Yt+1Y_{t+1} is added and attaches to an existing parent vertex Xt+1∈{Y1,…,Yt}X_{t+1}\in\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t}\} chosen by a randomized preferential rule described below.

Each vertex vv independently receives a permanent “attractiveness” label a​(v)∈{1,w}a(v)\in\{1,w\} with equal probability for the two options. The attractiveness-weighted degree of x∈Vtx\in V_{t} is

At​(x):=∑y∼txa​(y).A_{t}(x):=\sum_{y\sim_{t}x}a(y).

(Here ∼t\sim_{t} denotes adjacency at time tt.) The parent Xt+1X_{t+1} of Yt+1Y_{t+1} is chosen according to

ℙ​(Xt+1=x∣ℱt)=At​(x)St,St:=∑x∈VtAt​(x).\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}=x\mid\mathcal{F}_{t})=\frac{A_{t}(x)}{S_{t}},\qquad S_{t}:=\sum_{x\in V_{t}}A_{t}(x).

Here ℱt=σ​(G1,…,Gt)\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma(G_{1},\dots,G_{t}) is the associated filtration.

Our goal will be to approximately recover ww based on GtG_{t} for a single, large value of tt without observing the vertex labels. This was posed as an open problem333Importantly we note that this is the first COLT open problem that we tried with our scaffolded GPT-5. We chose this paper somewhat randomly, with some preference for it due to the authors’ familiarity with preferential attachment processes. at the 2012 Conference on Learning Theory in [54], who observed that single-edge label statistics do not help determine ww (in fact their question asks for a bit more, see Remark IV.4.1). This type of preferential attachment model was introduced in the seminal work [9] (in the case w=1w=1), with the aim of better modeling the emergence in real networks and explaining observed heavy-tailed behavior. Recovering ww amounts, in this simplified toy model, to a qualitatively interesting achievement: one has inferred the dynamical behavior of an evolving network while only observing the network at just 11 time. Note that there is a redundancy in the model above: reciprocating ww does not change the law of (Gt)t≥1(G_{t})_{t\geq 1} because one can reverse all the labels. Thus one should restrict to w≥1w\geq 1, and we correspondingly posed the following question to (a scaffolded version of) GPT-5 (see Figure IV.10).

GPT-5 was able to prove that ww is indeed identifiable, stated in Corollary IV.4.1 below. This is achieved by way of Theorem IV.4.1 below, which computes the limiting fraction f​(w)f(w) of vertices which are leaves at a given large time. To state the result, let L1​(t)L_{1}(t) (resp. Lw​(t)L_{w}(t)) be the number of leaves at time tt whose parent (unique neighbor) has attractiveness 11 (resp. ww). Then the total number L​(t)=L1​(t)+Lw​(t)L(t)=L_{1}(t)+L_{w}(t) of leaves at time tt is observable without observing the labels in GtG_{t} (while L1​(t)L_{1}(t) and Lw​(t)L_{w}(t) are not).

Theorem IV.4.1.

For any w>0w>0, one has almost surely:

limt→∞L​(t)t=f​(w)≡34−12​(w+2)+14​(2​w+1)=3​(w+1)22​(w+2)​(2​w+1).\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{L(t)}{t}=f(w)\equiv\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{2(w+2)}+\frac{1}{4(2w+1)}=\frac{3(w+1)^{2}}{2(w+2)(2w+1)}. (IV.6)

In fact, one has

limt→∞L(1)​(t)t=w+12​(w+2),limt→∞L(w)​(t)t=w+12​(2​w+1).\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{L^{(1)}(t)}{t}=\frac{w+1}{2(w+2)},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{L^{(w)}(t)}{t}=\frac{w+1}{2(2w+1)}.

The function ff defined in (IV.6) is easily seen to be strictly increasing, with

f′​(w)=12​(1(w+2)2−1(2​w+1)2)>0,∀w>1.f^{\prime}(w)=\frac{1}{2}\bigg(\frac{1}{(w+2)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(2w+1)^{2}}\bigg)>0,\quad\forall w>1.

Identifiability of ww is then immediate, as in the following Corollary.

Corollary IV.4.1.

For any w≥1w\geq 1 the point estimate w^​(t)=f−1​(L​(t)/t)\hat{w}(t)=f^{-1}(L(t)/t) converges to ww in probability as t→∞t\to\infty. Here f−1:[2/3,3/4]→[1,∞]f^{-1}:[2/3,3/4]\to[1,\infty] is the inverse of f|[1,∞]f|_{[1,\infty]}, and we set f−1​(x)=1f^{-1}(x)=1 for x≤2/3x\leq 2/3 and f−1​(x)=∞f^{-1}(x)=\infty for x≥3/4x\geq 3/4.

It is worth noting that the above type of algorithm provably fails in a related model of evolving trees studied in [11] (in which attachment probabilities depend only on label agreement and not on degree). In their model, the fraction of degree kk vertices is asymptotically 2−k2^{-k} for all parameter values. This illustrates that GPT-5’s decision to focus on the quantity L​(t)L(t) is already non-obvious.

Remark IV.4.1.

[54] in fact asks for a polynomial rate of convergence, i.e. an estimator w^​(t)\hat{w}(t) satisfying ℙ​[|w^​(t)−w|≤ε]≥1−δ\mathbb{P}[|\hat{w}(t)-w|\leq\varepsilon]\geq 1-\delta for tt polynomially large in (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta). We believe a more precise implementation of our approach suffices to show this stronger statement, but do not pursue this here. [54] also considers a slightly more general setting in which incoming vertices have probability pp to be labeled ww (which removes the convenient w↔1/ww\leftrightarrow 1/w symmetry).

Remark IV.4.2.

While all major proof ideas below are due to GPT-5, a few details of proof writing are human-supplied. Our scaffolded version of GPT-5 autonomously produced exactly the high-level argument below and the same main references, but omitted the proof details for certain intermediate assertions, stating (correctly) that they followed from routine stochastic approximation arguments. When we asked (an unscaffolded) GPT-5 to provide more detail for these latter arguments, it made several false starts, stating for example that [57, Theorem 1] directly implies Vt→0V_{t}\to 0 almost surely in the proof of Lemma IV.4.1 below, while it in fact only gives convergence of VtV_{t}. After some human pushback, GPT-5 eventually came up with a correct but unnecessarily complicated proof; we chose to present a more streamlined argument (by observing that 𝔼​[Vt]→0\mathbb{E}[V_{t}]\to 0).

IV.4.1 Proof Overview

We assume w≥1w\geq 1 without loss of generality, and treat ww as constant in all O​(⋅)O(\cdot) notation. Let

St(1):=∑x:a​(x)=1At​(x),St(w):=∑x:a​(x)=wAt​(x).S^{(1)}_{t}:=\sum_{x:a(x)=1}A_{t}(x),\qquad S^{(w)}_{t}:=\sum_{x:a(x)=w}A_{t}(x).

Then St(1)+St(w)=StS^{(1)}_{t}+S^{(w)}_{t}=S_{t}, and

Rt≡St(w)St=ℙ​[a​(Xt+1)=w]R_{t}\equiv\frac{S^{(w)}_{t}}{S_{t}}=\mathbb{P}[a(X_{t+1})=w]

is the chance for the next vertex to attach to a ww-labelled vertex in GtG_{t}. Further, let

Dt:=St(w)−12​St=St(w)−St(1)2=St⋅(Rt−12),μ=𝔼​[a​(new vertex)]=1+w2D_{t}:=S^{(w)}_{t}-\tfrac{1}{2}S_{t}=\frac{S_{t}^{(w)}-S_{t}^{(1)}}{2}=S_{t}\cdot(R_{t}-\tfrac{1}{2}),\qquad\mu=\mathbb{E}[a(\text{new vertex})]=\frac{1+w}{2} (IV.7)

and set (with Et=E​(Gt)E_{t}=E(G_{t}) the set of edges at time tt)

Tt:=∑{u,v}∈Eta​(u)​a​(v)=St(1)+w​St(w)2.T_{t}:=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_{t}}a(u)a(v)=\frac{S_{t}^{(1)}+wS_{t}^{(w)}}{2}.

Then

𝔼​[a​(Xt+1)∣ℱt]=2​TtSt.\mathbb{E}[a(X_{t+1})\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\frac{2T_{t}}{S_{t}}. (IV.8)

For notational convenience, given a discrete-time stochastic process (Zt)t≥1(Z_{t})_{t\geq 1} we write Δ​Zt=Zt+1−Zt\Delta Z_{t}=Z_{t+1}-Z_{t}.

The proof consists of two main steps. In the first we show Rt→1/2R_{t}\to 1/2 and St/t→w+1S_{t}/t\to w+1 almost surely (see Lemmas IV.4.1 and IV.4.2). In the second we use this to analyze the growth of L(1)​(t)L^{(1)}(t) and L(w)​(t)L^{(w)}(t). Both steps and especially the second employ classical stochastic approximation results in the style of [56, 57].

IV.4.2 One-Step Dynamics

When the (t+1)(t+1)-th vertex y=Yt+1y=Y_{t+1} attaches to the random vertex x=Xt+1∈{Y1,…,Yt}x=X_{t+1}\in\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t}\}, we have

Δ​At​(x)≡At+1​(x)−At​(x)=a​(y),Δ​At​(y)=a​(x),\Delta A_{t}(x)\equiv A_{t+1}(x)-A_{t}(x)=a(y),\qquad\Delta A_{t}(y)=a(x),

and At​(z)A_{t}(z) is unchanged for other vertices z∈{Y1,…,Yt}\{x}z\in\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t}\}\backslash\{x\}. Consequently

Δ​St=a​(x)+a​(y).\Delta S_{t}=a(x)+a(y).

Using (IV.8) one obtains with some algebra that

𝔼​[Δ​St∣ℱt]=μ+2​TtSt=Dt​(w−1)St+(w+1).\mathbb{E}[\Delta S_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\mu+\frac{2T_{t}}{S_{t}}=\frac{D_{t}(w-1)}{S_{t}}+(w+1). (IV.9)

Likewise,

Δ​St(w)=𝟏​{a​(x)=w}​a​(y)+𝟏​{a​(y)=w}​a​(x),\Delta S^{(w)}_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{a(x)=w\}a(y)+\mathbf{1}\{a(y)=w\}a(x),

and one can easily compute

𝔼​[Δ​Dt∣ℱt]=μ​(Rt−12)=μ​DtSt.\mathbb{E}[\Delta D_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\mu\big(R_{t}-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)=\frac{\mu D_{t}}{S_{t}}. (IV.10)

We also trivially have

2​t≤St≤2​w​t2t\leq S_{t}\leq 2wt (IV.11)

and |Δ​Rt|≤O​(1/St)|\Delta R_{t}|\leq O(1/S_{t}).

IV.4.3 Convergence of RtR_{t} and StS_{t}

Lemma IV.4.1.

limt→∞Rt=12\lim_{t\to\infty}R_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2} almost surely.

Proof.

Define

Vt:=(Rt−12)2=(Dt/St)2.V_{t}:=(R_{t}-\tfrac{1}{2})^{2}=(D_{t}/S_{t})^{2}.

We will show Vt→0V_{t}\to 0 holds almost surely. Letting Qt=Dt/StQ_{t}=D_{t}/S_{t}, one has

Δ​Vt=2​Qt​Δ​Qt+(Δ​Qt)2.\Delta V_{t}=2Q_{t}\Delta Q_{t}+(\Delta Q_{t})^{2}.

Next it is easy to see by Taylor’s approximation theorem that the quotient rule holds approximately for discrete differences; since |Δ​St(w)|,|Δ​St|≤O​(1)|\Delta S^{(w)}_{t}|,|\Delta S_{t}|\leq O(1) we find:

Δ​Qt\displaystyle\Delta Q_{t} =St​Δ​Dt−Dt​Δ​StSt2+O​(St−2).\displaystyle=\frac{S_{t}\Delta D_{t}-D_{t}\Delta S_{t}}{S_{t}^{2}}+O(S_{t}^{-2}).

Combining the previous two displays, we find:

Δ​Vt=2​DtSt2​(Δ​Dt−Dt​Δ​StSt)+O​(St−2).\Delta V_{t}=\frac{2D_{t}}{S_{t}^{2}}\Big(\Delta D_{t}-\frac{D_{t}\Delta S_{t}}{S_{t}}\Big)+O(S_{t}^{-2}).

Using (IV.10)–(IV.9) yields

𝔼​[Δ​Vt∣ℱt]=−4​Dt2​TtSt4+O​(St−2)=−Vt​(4​TtSt2)+O​(St−2).\mathbb{E}[\Delta V_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=-\frac{4D_{t}^{2}T_{t}}{S_{t}^{4}}+O(S_{t}^{-2})=-V_{t}\Big(\frac{4T_{t}}{S_{t}^{2}}\Big)+O(S_{t}^{-2}).

Since Tt≍St≍tT_{t}\asymp S_{t}\asymp t, we get

𝔼​[Δ​Vt∣ℱt]≤−Ω​(St−1)​Vt+O​(St−2).\mathbb{E}[\Delta V_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\leq-\Omega(S_{t}^{-1})V_{t}+O(S_{t}^{-2}).

By (IV.11), we have

∑t≥1St−1=∞,∑t≥1St−2=S¯​(w)<∞.\sum_{t\geq 1}S_{t}^{-1}=\infty,\qquad\sum_{t\geq 1}S_{t}^{-2}=\bar{S}(w)<\infty.

The almost-supermartingale theorem of [57, Theorem 1] implies that limt→∞Vt\lim_{t\to\infty}V_{t} exists almost surely. It remains to identify the limit. For this, letting Et=𝔼​[Vt]E_{t}=\mathbb{E}[V_{t}], we obtain

Et+1≤(1−c​St−1)​Et+O​(St−2).E_{t+1}\leq(1-cS_{t}^{-1})E_{t}+O(S_{t}^{-2}).

for a uniform constant c=c​(w)>0c=c(w)>0. Then

ET≤(E1+S¯​(w))⋅∏1≤t<T(1−c​St−1).E_{T}\leq(E_{1}+\bar{S}(w))\cdot\prod_{1\leq t<T}(1-cS_{t}^{-1}).

This tends to 0 as T→∞T\to\infty because ∑St−1=∞\sum S_{t}^{-1}=\infty. We conclude that Et→0E_{t}\to 0. Since Vt∈[0,1]V_{t}\in[0,1] for all tt, its almost-sure t→∞t\to\infty limit must therefore equal 0. This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma IV.4.2.

St/t→w+1S_{t}/t\to w+1 almost surely.

Proof.

Recalling (IV.9), we have

Δ​St=Dt​(w−1)St+(w+1)+ξt+1\Delta S_{t}=\frac{D_{t}(w-1)}{S_{t}}+(w+1)+\xi_{t+1}

for a bounded martingale difference ξt+1\xi_{t+1}. Since Dt/St→0D_{t}/S_{t}\to 0 from the previous lemma, Cesàro averaging yields

1t​∑i=1t(Dt​(w−1)St+(w+1))→w+1.\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\Big(\frac{D_{t}(w-1)}{S_{t}}+(w+1)\Big)\to w+1.

The martingale SLLN gives 1t​∑i=1tξi→0\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\xi_{i}\to 0 almost surely. Thus St/t→w+1S_{t}/t\to w+1. ∎

IV.4.4 Stochastic Approximation for Leaf Fractions

We use the following stochastic approximation result, which gives an ODE limit for certain stochastic processes. It follows by combining [12, Propositions 4.1 and 4.2] (using q=2q=2 therein), and specializing to a 11-dimensional state space.

Theorem IV.4.2.

Consider a scalar recursion

Zt+1=Zt+γt+1​(F​(Zt)+εt+1+δt+1)Z_{t+1}=Z_{t}+\gamma_{t+1}(F(Z_{t})+\varepsilon_{t+1}+\delta_{t+1})

driven by:

  • •

    Deterministic step sizes satisfying

    γt→0,∑t≥1γt=∞,∑t≥1γt2<∞.\gamma_{t}\to 0,\qquad\sum_{t\geq 1}\gamma_{t}=\infty,\qquad\sum_{t\geq 1}\gamma_{t}^{2}<\infty.
  • •

    A martingale-difference sequence (εt)t≥1(\varepsilon_{t})_{t\geq 1} adapted to a filtration ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} (i.e. 𝔼​[εt+1|ℱt]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t+1}|\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0) and satisfying 𝔼​[εt+12|ℱt]≤C\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t+1}^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{t}]\leq C for a deterministic constant CC.

  • •

    Asymptotically vanishing adapted perturbations: δt→0\delta_{t}\to 0 almost surely.

  • •

    Locally Lipschitz F:ℝ→ℝF:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}.

Suppose the ODE z′​(T)=F​(z​(T))z^{\prime}(T)=F(z(T)) has a unique globally attracting equilibrium z⋆z^{\star}, i.e. for all initial conditions z​(0)∈ℝz(0)\in\mathbb{R} one has limT→∞z​(T)=z⋆\lim_{T\to\infty}z(T)=z^{\star} for the solution to this ODE. Then almost surely the analogous convergence holds for the discrete system:

limt→∞Zt=z⋆.\lim_{t\to\infty}Z_{t}=z^{\star}.

Recall the definitions of L1​(t),Lw​(t)L_{1}(t),L_{w}(t) just above Theorem IV.4.1. It is easy to see that

𝔼​[Δ​L1∣ℱt]=St(1)−L1​(t)St,𝔼​[Δ​Lw∣ℱt]=St(w)−w​Lw​(t)St.\mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\frac{S_{t}^{(1)}-L_{1}(t)}{S_{t}},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{w}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\frac{S_{t}^{(w)}-wL_{w}(t)}{S_{t}}. (IV.12)

Indeed L1​(t)/StL_{1}(t)/S_{t} and Lw​(t)/StL_{w}(t)/S_{t} are the conditional probabilities (given ℱt)\mathcal{F}_{t}) for Xt+1X_{t+1} to be a leaf of label 11 and ww. On these events Xt+1X_{t+1} is no longer a leaf in Gt+1G_{t+1}.

The main quantities of interest will be the leaf fractions

xt=L1​(t)/t,yt=Lw​(t)/t.x_{t}=L_{1}(t)/t,\qquad y_{t}=L_{w}(t)/t.

Since e.g. xt+1=t​xtt+1x_{t+1}=\frac{tx_{t}}{t+1} when Δ​L1​(t)=0\Delta L_{1}(t)=0, we have:

Δ​xt=Δ​L1​(t)−xtt+1,Δ​yt=Δ​Lw​(t)−ytt+1.\Delta x_{t}=\frac{\Delta L_{1}(t)-x_{t}}{t+1},\qquad\Delta y_{t}=\frac{\Delta L_{w}(t)-y_{t}}{t+1}. (IV.13)

We showed in Lemma IV.4.1 and IV.4.2 above that almost surely

(St(1)t,St(w)t,Stt)→(w+12,w+12,w+1).\Big(\frac{S_{t}^{(1)}}{t},\frac{S_{t}^{(w)}}{t},\frac{S_{t}}{t}\Big)\to\Big(\frac{w+1}{2},\frac{w+1}{2},w+1\Big). (IV.14)

In light of (IV.12) and (IV.13), we will apply Theorem IV.4.2 to xtx_{t} and yty_{t} separately, with γt+1=1/(t+1)\gamma_{t+1}=1/(t+1) each in case. We use the vector fields

F1​(x)=12−x−x1+w,Fw​(y)=12−y−w​y1+w.F_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}-x-\frac{x}{1+w},\qquad F_{w}(y)=\frac{1}{2}-y-\frac{wy}{1+w}.

and the martingale noises

εt+1X:=Δ​L1​(t)−𝔼​[Δ​L1​(t)∣ℱt],εt+1Y:=Δ​Lw​(t)−𝔼​[Δ​Lw​(t)∣ℱt].\varepsilon_{t+1}^{X}:=\Delta L_{1}(t)-\mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{1}(t)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}],\qquad\varepsilon_{t+1}^{Y}:=\Delta L_{w}(t)-\mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{w}(t)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}].

Focusing without loss of generality on the xtx_{t} case, we obtain the recursion

xt+1=xt+γt+1​(F1​(xt)+εt+1X+δt+1X),x_{t+1}=x_{t}+\gamma_{t+1}(F_{1}(x_{t})+\varepsilon_{t+1}^{X}+\delta_{t+1}^{X}),

where δtX\delta_{t}^{X} is defined to make equality hold, and one has δtX→0\delta_{t}^{X}\to 0 almost surely as a consequence of (IV.14). Since |Δ​L1|≤1|\Delta L_{1}|\leq 1 almost surely, the required conditions on εtX\varepsilon_{t}^{X} are clear. It is also easy to see that the linear ODE x′​(T)=F1​(x​(T))x^{\prime}(T)=F_{1}(x(T)) has a unique stable, globally attracting fixed point, which is the zero of F1F_{1} given by

x⋆=w+12​(w+2).x^{\star}=\frac{w+1}{2(w+2)}.

Thus we may apply Theorem IV.4.2 to conclude the almost sure limit:

xt/t→w+12​(w+2).x_{t}/t\to\frac{w+1}{2(w+2)}.

Identical reasoning shows that yty_{t} converges almost surely to the unique zero of FwF_{w}, i.e.

yt/t→y⋆=w+12​(2​w+1).y_{t}/t\to y^{\star}=\frac{w+1}{2(2w+1)}.

This completes the proof of Theorem IV.4.1.

Conclusion

AI models are well-known for assisting with routine tasks; what is less well-known is that frontier models like GPT-5 are increasingly able to accelerate novel research. We highlighted examples across a range of scientific disciplines showing GPT-5 assisting in ideation, powering deep literature search, and even proposing and implementing proofs of (appropriately-sized) open problems. None of this would have been possible just twelve months ago. The fact that GPT-5 is already showing it can accelerate scientific research, combined with the rate of improvement of frontier AI, suggests that the coming years will be an exhilarating time in science and mathematics.
